questions.q: Per this lesson, why do most MDM programs actually get funded?
options: Because the topic is intellectually interesting to executives
Because bad master data is already costing the business in ways people can point to — duplicate outreach, blocked automation, inconsistent reporting
Because a vendor requires it as a condition of a software license
Because it is legally mandated in every industry
questions.explain: The lesson frames funding as driven by observable, existing costs — not abstract interest or universal legal mandate.

questions.q: Which of these is listed in this lesson as a cost of unmanaged master data?
options: Duplicate outreach to the same customer from multiple systems that each think they have the only record
Faster server response times
Lower electricity bills
Improved employee morale
questions.explain: Duplicate outreach — mailing or calling the same customer multiple times because systems don't share a unified view — is explicitly listed as a real cost.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say mergers and acquisitions commonly drive MDM investment?
options: M&A has no connection to master data at all
Combining two companies almost always means combining two separate, previously-incompatible sets of customers, products, and vendors
M&A always eliminates the need for master data management
M&A automatically resolves all duplicate records without any tooling
questions.explain: The lesson describes MDM as the practical mechanism for integrating two companies' master data without simply discarding one side's records.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should a credible MDM business case avoid doing?
options: Naming specific cost categories like duplicate outreach or inconsistent reporting
Referencing a real, specific example the organization has observed
Asserting a specific percentage ROI or an unverified industry statistic borrowed from elsewhere
Being written down at all
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against citing an unverified industry statistic or invented ROI figure, favoring the organization's own citable, specific pain instead.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the pitch that resonates most broadly across departments?
options: A single, trusted view of the customer (or product, or vendor) shared across sales, support, billing, and marketing
A promise to reduce headcount in every department
A guarantee of zero data entry errors forever
A commitment to switch database vendors
questions.explain: The lesson calls out the single/360-degree view as the broadest-landing pitch because it replaces several departments' inconsistent answers with one shared, trusted answer.
